title: Diversion headworks
summary: The weir versus barrage comparison is the most examined item, and the substance is that a barrage does its ponding with GATES on a low crest, giving better silt and flood control and less afflux, at higher cost. The three seepage theories form a progression worth understanding as such: Bligh counted total creep, Lane weighted the horizontal, and Khosla showed by potential flow that neither total creep nor intermediate sheet piles matter — only the exit gradient and the end piles do. Silt excluder versus ejector is the other reliable pairing.

sections.heading: Weir or barrage
sections.body:
A **diversion headwork** raises the water level in a river so that a canal can take off by gravity. It **diverts** but does **not store** — which is the distinction from a **dam**, and the first thing to establish.

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Weir / barrage** | **Diverts** — raises the level enough to command the canal |
| **Dam** | **Stores** — impounds a reservoir to regulate flow over time |

So a diversion headwork can supply water only when the river is flowing, which is why a run-of-river irrigation or hydropower scheme has no dry-season firm supply beyond the river's own low flow.

**Weir versus barrage — the comparison to memorise:**

| | **Weir** | **Barrage** |
|---|---|---|
| Crest | **Raised** — most of the ponding is done by the crest itself | **Low** — most of the ponding is done by **GATES** |
| Ponding controlled by | The **fixed crest**, with shutters on top | **Adjustable gates** over the full width |
| **Afflux** (upstream rise in flood) | **Higher** | **Lower** — gates are opened, so the obstruction is small |
| **Flood control** | Poor — the crest obstructs the flood | **Good** — gates pass the flood freely |
| **Silt control** | Poor | **Good** — gates can be operated to sluice silt through |
| Level control | Coarse | **Fine and adjustable** |
| **Cost** | **Lower** | **Higher** — gates, hoists, piers, operating platform |
| Operation | Minimal | **Needs staff and power** |
| Roadway | Not usually | **Often carries a road or rail bridge** |

**The barrage's advantages all come from the same source: the gates.** Because the ponding is done by adjustable gates on a low crest, the structure can be **opened out** in flood — so it obstructs the river far less, produces less **afflux** and therefore less upstream submergence, and needs lower marginal embankments. The same gates allow **silt to be sluiced downstream** rather than accumulating in the pond.

Its costs are equally direct: gates, hoisting gear, piers, an operating platform and — decisively — **trained staff to operate it**. A barrage whose gates are not operated correctly performs worse than a weir, because its low crest cannot pond the water on its own.

**That operational dependence is why the choice is not purely economic.** A barrage suits a site with reliable staffing and power; a weir suits a remote site where operation cannot be assured. In Nepal both exist, and the smaller hill diversions are almost always weirs for exactly that reason.

**Site selection for a diversion headwork:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| A **narrow, well-defined river section** | Shortest and cheapest structure |
| **Stable banks**, not a meandering reach | The river must not move away from the works |
| A **straight reach**, or the **concave** bank for the intake | Deep water at the intake; silt deposits on the convex side |
| **Sound foundation** — rock preferred | Reduces seepage and scour problems |
| **Adequate command** for the canal | The pond level must be above the canal FSL |
| Accessible for construction and operation | — |
| Minimum submergence and acquisition upstream | Afflux affects land and property |

**Placing the intake on the concave (outer) bank of a bend** is worth understanding: in a river bend the **helical secondary current** carries the **bed load toward the convex (inner) bank**, where a point bar forms, while the **outer bank is scoured and the water is deep**. An intake on the outer bank therefore draws **deeper, cleaner water** — a free advantage from the river's own hydraulics.

sections.heading: Components of a diversion headwork
sections.body:
| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Weir or barrage** | Raises the water level across the river |
| **Under-sluices** | A **deeper bay adjacent to the head regulator**, with its own crest lower than the weir; **scours the silt** from the pocket and passes low flows |
| **Divide wall** | Separates the under-sluice pocket from the weir bays, creating **still water in front of the regulator** |
| **Canal head regulator** | Controls the discharge admitted to the canal, and excludes silt and floods |
| **Fish ladder** | Allows **fish migration** past the obstruction |
| **Silt excluder** | In the river bed **before** the regulator; excludes the silt-laden bottom layer |
| **River training works** | Guide banks, marginal embankments, spurs — confine the river to the works |
| **Impervious floor and cut-offs** | Resist **seepage, uplift and scour** |
| **Energy dissipation** — cistern, blocks, apron | Kills the energy of the flow passing over |

**The divide wall repays understanding**, because its function is not obvious. Separating the under-sluice pocket from the weir bays creates a **quiet, still pocket** in front of the head regulator. In still water the **silt settles out** before reaching the canal intake, and the accumulated silt is then **flushed downstream through the under-sluices**. So the divide wall and the under-sluices work as a pair: one creates the settling pocket, the other empties it.

The divide wall also **prevents cross-currents** in front of the regulator and separates the flow of the two very differently sized bays.

**Under-sluices** serve three purposes at once: they **scour the silt** from the pocket, they **pass the low flow** of the dry season (keeping the river channel near the intake alive), and in flood they **pass a large discharge** through the deeper bay. Their crest is set **lower** than the weir crest — typically at or near the river bed — which is what allows them to scour.

**The fish ladder** is a genuine requirement, not a formality, on Nepal's rivers, where migratory species move seasonally between the plains and the hills. It works by dividing the total drop into many **small steps or pools**, each with a drop small enough for a fish to negotiate, with a velocity that fish can swim against (typically limited to about 2 m/s in the passage). A ladder that is hydraulically wrong — too steep, too fast, or dry at low flow — is worse than none, because it appears to discharge the obligation without doing so.

**Canal head regulator** duties: **control the discharge** into the canal, **exclude silt** (by having its crest raised above the river bed, so it skims the cleaner upper layer), **exclude floods**, and **permit closure** for canal maintenance. It is provided with gates, and its crest level is a design decision balancing command against silt exclusion.

**Silt excluder or silt ejector — the pairing questions ask:**

| | **Silt EXCLUDER** | **Silt EJECTOR (extractor)** |
|---|---|---|
| Located | In the **river bed, UPSTREAM of the head regulator** | **In the canal**, downstream of the regulator |
| Function | **Prevents silt ENTERING** the canal | **Removes silt ALREADY ADMITTED** |
| Principle | The **bottom layer carries most of the sediment**; tunnels divert that layer downstream through the under-sluices | Silt is concentrated at the bed and drawn off through a tunnel back to the river |
| Preference | **Better — prevention** | The fallback where exclusion is incomplete |

**The principle both rely on is the same**, and it is the reason they work at all: **sediment concentration is far higher near the bed** than near the surface, because gravity keeps the coarser particles low. So separating the bottom layer separates most of the sediment. An excluder does that **before** the canal, an ejector **after**.

**Prevention before cure** is the design preference: an excluder keeps the silt out of the canal entirely, whereas an ejector must first admit it and then spend water to remove it — the ejector's escape flow being water diverted and then returned unused.

sections.heading: Seepage theories and the design of the impervious floor
sections.body:
**The problem.** A weir or barrage founded on **permeable alluvium** creates a head difference between the upstream pond and the downstream river. Water therefore **seeps under the structure**, and it causes two distinct failures:

| Failure | Mechanism | Guarded against by |
|---|---|---|
| **PIPING (undermining)** | The **exit gradient** at the downstream end is high enough to **lift and carry away soil particles**, and erosion works backward along a "pipe" until the structure is undermined | **Lengthening the seepage path** (cut-offs, sheet piles, upstream apron) and providing an **inverted filter** at the exit |
| **UPLIFT (floor rupture)** | The **seepage pressure under the floor exceeds its weight**, and the floor is lifted and ruptured | **Adequate floor THICKNESS** |

So the two failures need two different remedies — **length** for piping, **thickness** for uplift — and that distinction organises the whole of the design.

**Bligh's creep theory (1910)** — the first attempt:

> **Creep length L = the SUM of all horizontal and vertical paths along the base**, all taken as **equally effective**
> **Head loss is assumed to be UNIFORM along the creep length**, giving a hydraulic gradient of **H/L**
> **Safe creep length L = C × H**, with Bligh's coefficient C = 4 to 18 by soil type
> **Floor thickness t = (h/(G − 1)) × 4/3**, with h the uplift head at that point

**Its defects** are what motivated the successors: it assumes **horizontal and vertical creep are equally effective** (they are not — vertical paths are more effective per unit length), it assumes a **uniform** hydraulic gradient (the real gradient is far from uniform, being steepest at the exit), and it takes **no account of the exit gradient** as such.

**Lane's weighted creep theory (1935)** made one correction:

> **Weighted creep length L_w = (1/3) × horizontal creep + vertical creep**

So Lane weighted **horizontal creep at only one third** of vertical creep, recognising from a wider survey of dam failures that vertical cut-offs are the more effective. It remains empirical, and still ignores the exit gradient.

**Khosla's theory of independent variables (1936)** — a genuine advance, because it used **potential flow theory** rather than observation.

Khosla and his associates, investigating failures on the Upper Chenab Canal, solved the **Laplace equation** for seepage beneath a floor with sheet piles, and reached conclusions that overturned the earlier theories:

| Khosla's finding | Consequence |
|---|---|
| The **actual pressure distribution differs greatly** from Bligh's uniform assumption | Bligh's method could be unsafe at some points and wasteful at others |
| **The EXIT GRADIENT** is what governs piping — not the total creep length | Design against a **safe exit gradient**, not a creep coefficient |
| **The OUTER FACES of the END sheet piles are far more effective** than the inner faces | Put the piles at the ends |
| **INTERMEDIATE sheet piles below the floor are LARGELY INEFFECTIVE** if shorter than the end piles | Money spent on them is largely wasted |
| An **upstream pile** reduces uplift; a **downstream pile** reduces the exit gradient | Each end pile has a distinct role |

**The exit gradient** for a floor of length b with a downstream cut-off of depth d:

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π √λ)**,  where **λ = (1 + √(1 + α²))/2** and **α = b/d**

**Safe exit gradients:**

| Material | Safe G_E |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1/5 to 1/6** |
| **Fine sand** | **1/6 to 1/7** |

Finer material needs a flatter gradient, because its particles are lighter and more easily lifted.

**Floor thickness from uplift.** At any point, the uplift head h (from the pressure distribution) must be balanced by the floor's weight:

> **t = h / (G − 1)**  with G the specific gravity of the floor material (about 2.24 for concrete under water)

and a **factor of safety of about 1.33** is applied, giving **t = (4/3) × h/(G − 1)**.

**The thickness is therefore greatest where the uplift head is greatest**, which is at the **upstream end of the downstream floor** — just downstream of the crest. That is why the downstream floor tapers, being thick near the structure and thinner toward its end.

**Khosla's pressure curves** give the pressure at key points (the corners and pile tips) for the standard configurations — a straight floor with an end pile, a floor with a pile at either end — and **corrections** are then applied for the **floor thickness**, the **mutual interference** of piles, and the **slope of the floor**.

**The inverted filter** at the downstream exit is the other essential protection, and its logic is elegant: it is **graded coarse to fine downward**, so it is **coarse where the water leaves** (offering no resistance to flow) and **fine against the soil** (preventing particles being carried out). It thus **relieves the pressure while retaining the soil** — the same principle as a drainage filter behind a retaining wall. Over it is placed a **launching apron** of loose stone, which launches itself down the scour slope as the bed erodes.

**Scour depth** must be computed to fix the depth of the cut-offs and the extent of the aprons, from **Lacey's formula**:

> **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}**  for a river of unrestricted width, or **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** in terms of discharge per unit width

with multipliers of **1.25 to 2.0** at a nose, a pier or a curved head. **Cut-offs and foundations must extend below the maximum anticipated scour**, plus a grip length — because a structure founded above the scour level will be undermined in the first large flood.

sections.heading: Energy dissipation, afflux and weir types
sections.body:
**Energy dissipation.** Water passing over a weir or through a barrage arrives downstream with a large **excess of energy**, which will scour the river bed if it is not dissipated in a controlled place.

The standard means is a **hydraulic jump** formed in a concrete **cistern (stilling basin)** immediately downstream:

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Glacis** | The sloping face on which the jump forms |
| **Cistern** | The depressed floor containing the jump |
| **Friction / baffle blocks** | Increase turbulence, shorten the jump, stabilise its position |
| **End sill** | Deflects the residual current upward, away from the bed |
| **Inverted filter and launching apron** | Protect the transition to the natural bed |

**The design condition** is that the **tailwater level must match the sequent depth y₂** of the jump. If the tailwater is **too low**, the jump **sweeps downstream out of the cistern** and dissipates its energy by scouring the river bed instead. If **too high**, the jump is **submerged** and dissipates less energy, with a fast current running along the bed.

Since the tailwater level varies with the river discharge, the cistern must be checked for **several flow conditions**, and the critical case is often **not the maximum flood** but an intermediate flow where the head is high and the tailwater still low. That is a standard examination point and a real design trap.

The jump relations: **y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)** and **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂)**, with the **steady jump range Fr₁ = 4.5 to 9.0** being the design target.

**Afflux** is the **rise in upstream water level** caused by the obstruction:

> It determines the **height of the marginal embankments**, the **extent of upstream submergence**, and hence the **land to be acquired**.

**Molesworth's formula** is the classical estimate for afflux at a constricted waterway. A **barrage produces markedly less afflux than a weir** for the same pond level, because its gates can be opened in flood — which is one of its principal advantages and often the deciding factor where upstream land is valuable or populated.

**Marginal (guide) embankments** confine the afflux-raised water so it does not spread over the countryside upstream, and **guide banks** direct the river through the waterway. Both are river training works, treated in the next subchapter.

**Waterway.** The clear width provided for the river:

> **Lacey's regime perimeter P = 4.75 √Q** gives the natural width, and the waterway is generally provided at about **1.0 to 1.2 times** that value

Providing **less** waterway increases afflux, velocity and scour; providing **more** costs money and encourages silting and meandering within the works. The **looseness factor** (waterway provided ÷ Lacey's perimeter) expresses the choice.

**Types of weir by construction:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Vertical drop (masonry / concrete)** | A solid wall with a cistern below; **simple**, suits a **firm clay or rock** foundation; the oldest type |
| **Rockfill (dry stone) weir** | Boulders laid in slopes; **cheap where stone is abundant**, suits a **wide river with a small drop**; needs a long apron |
| **Concrete glacis (sloping) weir** | A sloping downstream glacis on which a **hydraulic jump forms** — **the modern standard** |
| **Parabolic glacis** | A refinement of the above |

**The sloping glacis weir is the modern choice** for the reason given above: the **hydraulic jump forms on the glacis in a known, controlled position**, where a concrete cistern with blocks and an end sill can be provided to contain it. In a vertical drop weir the jump position is less predictable and the impact on the cistern floor more severe.

**Weir crest control:**

| Arrangement | Character |
|---|---|
| **Fixed crest** | Simplest; the pond level is fixed by the crest |
| **Falling shutters** | Raise the pond in the dry season and **fall in flood**, reducing afflux; manual or automatic |
| **Gated (barrage)** | Full control |

**Falling shutters** are the intermediate solution and a neat one: a shutter raises the effective crest and thus the pond level when water is needed, and **falls automatically** (by design of its hinge and counterweight) when the flood level rises — restoring the low crest and reducing afflux exactly when that matters. Their weakness is unreliability: a shutter that fails to fall causes the afflux it exists to prevent, and one that fails to rise loses the command.

**The complete design sequence** for a diversion headwork, to hold the parts together:

1. Fix the **pond level** from the canal's command requirement.
2. Fix the **waterway** from Lacey's perimeter and the looseness factor.
3. Fix the **crest level and shape**, and the **discharge capacity** for the design flood.
4. Compute the **afflux** and set the **marginal embankment** levels.
5. Compute the **scour depth** (Lacey) and fix the **cut-off depths and apron extents**.
6. Analyse **seepage by Khosla's method** — pressures, exit gradient, floor thickness.
7. Design the **energy dissipation** — glacis, cistern, blocks, end sill — checked for several flow conditions.
8. Design the **under-sluices, divide wall, head regulator, fish ladder and silt excluder**.
9. Design the **river training works**.

Each step feeds the next, and step 7's dependence on step 5's tailwater estimate is the link most often mishandled.

formulas.label: Bligh's creep theory
formulas.expression: L = Σ(horizontal + vertical creep), all equally weighted ;   safe L = C × H ;   t = (4/3)·h/(G−1)
formulas.note: Assumes a UNIFORM hydraulic gradient H/L and ignores the exit gradient — its principal defects.

formulas.label: Lane's weighted creep
formulas.note: Weights horizontal creep at one third, recognising that vertical cut-offs are more effective.

formulas.label: Khosla's exit gradient
formulas.note: Safe values: 1/4–1/5 shingle, 1/5–1/6 coarse sand, 1/6–1/7 fine sand.

formulas.label: Floor thickness from uplift
formulas.expression: t = h/(G − 1), with a factor of safety ≈ 1.33 giving t = (4/3)h/(G − 1)
formulas.note: Greatest where the uplift head is greatest — just downstream of the crest.

formulas.label: Lacey scour depth
formulas.expression: R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3} ;   or R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} per unit width
formulas.note: Multiply by 1.25–2.0 at a nose, pier or curved head. Cut-offs must go BELOW maximum scour.

formulas.label: Lacey waterway
formulas.note: The ratio is the looseness factor. Too little waterway raises afflux, velocity and scour.

formulas.label: Hydraulic jump in the cistern
formulas.note: The tailwater must MATCH y₂. Check several flow conditions — the critical case is often not the peak flood.

formulas.label: Silt excluder and ejector
formulas.expression: Excluder: in the RIVER, before the regulator — prevents entry. Ejector: in the CANAL — removes admitted silt.
formulas.note: Both exploit the fact that sediment concentration is highest near the bed.
